subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Well-to-Wheel Efficiency
description: A quick win: understand Well-to-Wheel Efficiency.

hook.text: Comparing a gas car to an EV isn't fair unless you count all the energy used from source to wheels.

buildup.text: A gas car's chain: drill oil, refine it, truck it, pump it, burn it. Each step loses energy.

discovery.text: An EV's chain: generate electricity, transmit it, charge the battery, drive. Fewer loss points overall.

twist.text: If the electricity comes from coal, an EV's total efficiency advantage shrinks dramatically.

climax.text: On a clean grid, an EV is about 3 times more efficient well-to-wheel than a gas car.

punchline.text: The real comparison starts at the energy source, not the tailpipe.

quiz.question: On a clean grid, how much more efficient is an EV well-to-wheel?

details.summary: Well-to-wheel efficiency measures the total energy lost from extracting a fuel source to actually moving the car's wheels, accounting for drilling, refining, transport, and engine or motor losses.
details.whyItMatters: Comparing only tailpipe emissions is misleading. Well-to-wheel analysis reveals the true environmental cost of each powertrain, showing EVs are typically 2 to 3 times more efficient overall.
takeaways: Gasoline cars convert about 20 percent of fuel energy to wheel motion
EVs convert 60 to 80 percent of grid electricity to wheel motion
Hydrogen fuel cells fall between gasoline and battery EVs in efficiency

faq.question: Does the electricity source change an EV's well-to-wheel efficiency?
faq.answer: Yes significantly. An EV charged from coal power has much higher upstream emissions than one charged from renewables. As grids get cleaner, EVs become even more efficient relative to fossil fuels.

faq.question: Why are combustion engines so inefficient?
faq.answer: Most of the fuel's energy is lost as heat through the exhaust, cooling system, and engine block. Thermodynamic limits mean even the best gasoline engines waste about 60 percent of fuel energy as heat.
